latest.title: Electrolysis Applications
latest.summary: Industrial applications: extraction of aluminium from bauxite (Hall-Héroult process), copper refining, electroplating with chromium/silver, and brine electrolysis.

latest.title: Ions and Ionic Bonds
latest.summary: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions held in a giant ionic lattice by strong electrostatic forces.

latest.title: Uses of Sulfur Compounds
latest.summary: Sulfuric acid is the most manufactured chemical: used in fertilisers, detergents, paints, plastics, metal processing, and as an electrolyte in car batteries.

latest.title: Energetics of Reactions
latest.summary: Exothermic reactions release heat to surroundings (ΔH negative). Endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH positive). Energy level diagrams show relative energies.

latest.title: Indicators and pH
latest.summary: pH scale (0-14): <7 acidic, 7 neutral, >7 alkaline. Universal indicator shows full range. Litmus, methyl orange, and phenolphthalein have specific colour changes.

latest.title: Experimental Techniques
latest.summary: Methods for separating and purifying substances including chromatography, distillation, filtration, crystallisation, and determining purity.

latest.title: Making Salts
latest.summary: Salts are produced by neutralising acids with metals, bases, or carbonates. Soluble salts prepared by titration or acid+excess solid; insoluble salts by precipitation.

latest.title: Acids and Bases
latest.summary: Acids are proton (H⁺) donors; bases are proton acceptors. Strong acids fully dissociate in water; weak acids partially dissociate. Common laboratory acids: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃.

latest.title: Rusting of Iron
latest.summary: Rusting requires oxygen AND water. Prevention methods: barrier protection (paint, oil, plastic, tin-plating), sacrificial protection (galvanising with zinc), and alloying (stainless steel).

latest.title: Group 7 Halogens
latest.summary: Group 7 elements (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) are diatomic non-metals. Reactivity decreases down the group. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide salt.

latest.title: Rates of Reaction
latest.summary: Reaction rate depends on concentration, temperature, surface area, and catalysts. Explained by collision theory — particles must collide with sufficient energy (activation energy) and correct orientation.
